transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-09-06
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Chris (Redwood SE), Lina (CTO Helmwave), Rajiv (SRE), Emily (Security)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Helmwave wants to run Redwood Private in their VPCs across three regions with a PrivateLink 'mesh' pattern. Primary concerns: cross-account PrivateLink attachments, egress NAT behavior, DNS resolution for private endpoints, MTU and packet fragmentation when transit peering to on-prem, and how KV cache warming and batching affect p99 latency. They discussed a pilot plan and next steps to share network diagrams, run benchmarks, and review security docs.

Topics:
- PrivateLink mesh topology options
- NAT-peering / egress behavior and hairpin avoidance
- DNS resolver strategy for private endpoints and split-horizon
- KV cache warmup, batching windows, and quantization impact on throughput
- On-prem transit MTU and TCP reassembly concerns

Action items (captured above)

Transcript: (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect)
[00:00:00] Maya (AE): All right, thanks everyone for jumping on. Lina, Rajiv, Emily, thanks for making time. We're planning to focus on PrivateLink mesh and the networking/kv-batching interactions today.
[00:00:18] Lina (CTO): Thanks. We want to validate two things -- first that we can keep inference traffic inside our accounts and second that we don't see p99 regressions when KV cache is warm versus cold. Also, we have strict egress policies, so the NAT behavior is important.
[00:00:35] Chris (SE): Yep, makes sense. Quick agenda: propose three topologies, look at egress/NAT choices for each, then discuss how the runtime's KV cache + batching affect client-side latency and suggestions for quantization.
[00:00:50] Rajiv (SRE): Curious, when you say "mesh" — do you mean many-to-many PrivateLink attachments or transit via a central VPC? Our infra team prefers minimal route table changes.
[00:01:06] Chris (SE): Great question. We sketched two variants: (A) fully meshed PrivateLink attachments across accounts, which gives direct interface endpoints in each account; and (B) a hub-and-spoke using a peering/transit gateway where the Redwood Private control plane sits in the hub. Variant A avoids transit hairpin but has more PrivateLink objects to manage.
[00:01:27] Lina: Does variant A blow up on the AWS quota side? We have a lot of accounts.
[00:01:33] Chris: It can. There are account-level limits for interface endpoints; you can request increases but it adds operational overhead. For large orgs we often recommend a hybrid: direct PrivateLink to high-traffic accounts and hub transit for low-volume ones.
[00:01:48] Emily (Security): Also on the security side, we need mTLS enforced and SNI filtering. Can PrivateLink support certificate pinning to the Redwood side?
[00:01:58] Chris: PrivateLink is L4 but your mTLS terminates at the Redwood service. We support mutual TLS with client certs and you can enforce SNI on the listener. We'll document the cert rotation flows.
[00:02:12] Rajiv: About egress: our current pattern is to force all egress through a central NAT gateway and egress proxy. That means the source IP changes, which breaks host-based allowlists on some downstreams. How would Redwood calls appear to the rest of our infra?
[00:02:27] Maya: If you route outbound to the internet via NAT, Redwood's outbound calls (for optional telemetry or artifact pulls) will come from that NAT IP unless you use VPC endpoints for the specific services. For Private deployments you can disable outbound entirely and Redwood will operate without external egress except what you explicitly grant.
[00:02:45] Lina: We want no outbound. But we need to be sure that model downloads, kernel updates, and healthchecks don't try to go out.
[00:02:54] Chris: Right — we offer an air-gapped packaging option where we pre-stage model artifacts into an S3 bucket you control or into local storage. We also provide an offline update mechanism. For health checks, we can keep them inside the VPC.
[00:03:10] Rajiv: Good. Now on to MTU and on-prem. We observed fragmentation when we traced packets across our MPLS to colo — packets larger than 1500 were getting dropped intermittently. Any opinion on the runtime's packet size expectations?
[00:03:25] Chris: The runtime isn't sensitive to MTU except for large gRPC streaming frames and bulk KV transfers during cold starts. We recommend enabling TCP MSS clamping on the peering devices and setting the interface MTU conservatively (e.g., 1400–1450) if your transit has unknown MTU behavior. Also, keep gRPC window sizes conservative to avoid IP fragmentation.
[00:03:48] Emily: So for the KV cache warmup, what's the pattern exactly? If we have many cold sessions, do we see a p99 spike?
[00:03:56] Chris: Yes, cold KV cache misses can add tens to low hundreds of milliseconds depending on model and sequence length. Our runtime uses asynchronous prefetching for likely prefixes and continuous batching to reduce per-token overhead. But if your workload opens many short lived connections that never reuse the KV cache, you get higher p99.
[00:04:17] Rajiv: Can we reuse KV caches across requests from different accounts if they're all talking to the same model? We want to amortize memory.
[00:04:25] Chris: For tenant isolation, caches are per-customer. You can shard caches per-model and per-workload within your account. We don't share across accounts for security. However, within a dedicated pool you can configure larger shared caches that are scoped to the Dedicated capacity. That's a common tradeoff: isolation vs memory efficiency.
[00:04:44] Lina: On batching: our client usage has a lot of small requests. How aggressive is Redwood's batching window? Will batching increase latency for single-user interactions?
[00:04:55] Chris: Batching is adaptive. For low QPS paths we keep small batching windows (milliseconds) so single-user latency doesn't suffer. For high QPS, we batch more aggressively. You can pin SLOs per route and we will prioritize latency-sensitive routes with smaller windows and dedicated workers.
[00:05:12] Rajiv: Any knobs to force 'no-batch' for certain routes?
[00:05:16] Chris: Yes, per-route config you can set batching:false and also set a maximum batching window and maximum batch size. But note: no-batch is more expensive per token.
[00:05:27] Emily: About quantization—if we use int8 quantized weights, are there tradeoffs for latency or KV cache size? We want to squeeze memory on on-prem GPU boxes.
[00:05:36] Chris: Quantization reduces model memory footprint and usually reduces per-token compute time on accelerator paths that support int8 kernels. However, quantization can slightly change model output characteristics which impacts cache hit usefulness: if tokenization or logits drift, your prefix-based cache may miss more often. We recommend running a small eval suite to check output quality before full rollout.
[00:05:58] Lina: Makes sense. How do drops and retries interact with batching and cache warmup? We saw our load balancer retry a few requests and that caused duplicate cache population and unexpected spikes.
[00:06:11] Chris: Retries are tricky. We try to dedupe idempotent token generation requests at the runtime layer when possible, but duplicate client retries can create cache pollution. The recommendation: set client-side retry windows to be conservative (exponential backoff) and enable request-idempotency tokens so we can detect duplicates server-side. We'll include a sample client middleware.
[00:06:29] Speaker 2 (auto label, likely Rajiv): if we do transit gateway in hub, does that mean traffic will hairpin through hub? For example, account A talks to account B via hub, does the packet path bounce?
[00:06:41] Chris: Yes, hub will centralize traffic and it might traverse the hub twice depending on routing; that's where MTU and latency considerations matter. For critical low-latency paths we prefer direct PrivateLink attachments.
[00:06:53] Rajiv: Any recommendations for DNS? Split horizon, Route53 inbound endpoints etc?
[00:06:58] Chris: For private endpoints we recommend a split-horizon approach: create private hosted zones in each account and use conditional forwarding to an internal resolver for the Redwood domain. Alternatively, you can point to the Redwood interface endpoint IPs directly in the VPC's resolver rules. We also support resolving via customer-provided DNS over the PrivateLink interface endpoint.
[00:07:19] Emily: How do we audit calls? We need immutable logs for every inference request for compliance.
[00:07:24] Maya: We have request-level telemetry retained per your retention policy. For Private deployments you can push logs to your S3/Kinesis or keep them in the control plane with long retention as an add-on. We'll walk through the schema; it contains hashed prompt identifiers (optionally) to avoid storing PII.
[00:07:42] Lina: Okay, can we look at a concrete pilot plan? We want to run a three-day pilot that measures p95/p99 for a synthetic chat workload and a production-weighted workload that hits KV-heavy prefixes.
[00:07:54] Chris: Absolutely. Suggested pilot steps: 1) You share CIDRs, account IDs, and a small test VPC we can use; 2) we deploy a dedicated trial pool or spin up a private on-prem image in your lab; 3) run the benchmark script we provide — it primes the KV cache and measures cold vs warm latency, bandwidth, and CPU/GPU utilization; 4) we iterate.
[00:08:17] Rajiv: For step 2, do we need to open outbound 443 to Redwood for orchestration?
[00:08:22] Chris: Not necessarily. We can operate with a control plane proxy in your VPC or do an air-gapped handshake where we exchange a bootstrap bundle. The only time we need outbound is if you opt into managed model downloads.
[00:08:33] Emily: Security wants to review KMS integration. Do you support HSM-backed keys and cross-account CMKs?
[00:08:40] Maya: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM solutions and support cross-account CMK usage for the Private control plane. We'll include configuration examples for AWS KMS and notes for GCP Cloud KMS.
[00:08:55] Lina: A few small things we noticed in the test lab: when the KV cache was being repopulated it caused bursts of egress to our internal metrics collector, which tripped rate limits. Any mitigation?
[00:09:08] Chris: You can throttle telemetry or buffer it locally and ship at a controlled rate; for the pilot we can enable sampling. Also, pre-warm the KV cache during maintenance windows so the cold-warm transition doesn't coincide with peak telemetry periods.
[00:09:21] Rajiv: Example timeline and milestones?
[00:09:23] Maya: Proposed timeline: 1 week to align network details and get artifacts; 1 week to stand up the pilot infra; 3 days of running benchmarks; 1 week to analyze and produce a recommendation. So roughly 4–5 weeks end-to-end if ready now.
[00:09:39] Lina: That works. Are there any gotchas we should know about for on-prem GPUs — driver versions, NCCL, or kernel compatibility?
[00:09:48] Chris: For on-prem we publish a compatibility matrix. Main things: CUDA/cuDNN versions must match the runtime's kernel set; NCCL is used for multi-GPU scaling and you should enable the recommended network MTU. We also advise isolating inference nodes from noisy neighbors and pinning CPU cores for the runtime process.
[00:10:06] Emily: One more compliance question: can logs be redacted automatically to remove PII before being stored?
[00:10:12] Maya: Yes — we offer built-in redaction hooks and can run a customer-side filter before logs leave your VPC. We'll share the redaction patterns and examples.
[00:10:23] Speaker 3 (auto): quick aside, competitor question — are you folks doing anything special to beat BigCloud AI on cold-starts?
[00:10:31] Chris: We tune the runtime for prefix caching and streaming so you get partial outputs quickly. Our KV cache design and continuous batching is intended to reduce cold p99. But we'll share benchmark numbers that are configurable per deployment.
[00:10:45] Rajiv: Ok let's recap the concrete asks — subnet diagram + suggested interfaces, the benchmark script, SOC2/KMS docs, and a lab date.
[00:10:54] Maya: Correct. Chris will generate the diagram. Lina will share network details. I'll send the compliance docs and quote. We'll target lab week of Sep 18.
[00:11:05] Lina: Sounds good, thanks.
[00:11:08] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up by email and post the artifacts to the shared Confluence link.

(remaining minutes spent on quick Q&A and clarifications; end of call)
